docs.title: QRadar Offense Intelligence
docs.text:
AI-powered SOC investigation platform for IBM QRadar. On-device LLM analysis · MITRE ATT&CK mapping · Campaign detection · Zero data egress.

Offense Detail — AI analysis verdict, MITRE kill chain, and structured investigation workspace.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
QRadar Offense Intelligence is a native IBM QRadar application that transforms how SOC teams investigate, manage, and respond to security offenses.

QRadar surfaces offenses with raw metadata — rule names, source IPs, event counts. Turning that into a confident verdict requires an analyst to manually query events, look up rule logic, cross-reference historical patterns, and consult runbooks. At scale, this takes 30 minutes to several hours per offense and becomes the primary bottleneck in Mean Time to Respond (MTTR).

QRadar Offense Intelligence eliminates that bottleneck. It embeds the Qwen3.5-9B large language model, running locally via llama.cpp directly on the QRadar appliance, and delivers a structured AI threat analysis — verdict, kill chain, recommended actions. No security data ever leaves the customer's environment.

docs.title: Core Capabilities
docs.text:
• On-Device AI Analysis

    The LLM runs entirely on your QRadar appliance. Structured 7-section threat analysis per offense — verdict, attack narrative, MITRE mapping, affected assets, recommended actions, false positive assessment, and executive summary.

  • MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

    Automatic technique tagging via on-device LLM, validated against a local ATT&CK knowledge base. Analyst overrides and team knowledge base promotion. Full offline support.

  • Attack Campaign Detection

    Automatically clusters related offenses into named attack campaigns. Each campaign shows a kill chain progression, date range, severity, analyst assignments, and lateral movement warnings.

  • Relationship Graph

    Interactive network graph with 5 investigative lenses: Rule Topology, Attacker Topology, Target Topology, Campaign Topology, and Lateral Movement chain.

  • Investigation Workspace

    Collaborative notes, evidence file attachments, IOC artifact tracking, response task lists, and SOP playbooks — all bound to the offense inside QRadar.

  • SLA Management & Analytics

    Real-time MTTD, MTTR, MTTA tracking, SLA breach notifications, analyst workload distribution, and stalled case identification.

docs.title: Key Differentiator
docs.text:
Zero Data Egress

The AI model (Qwen3.5-9B Q5) runs on the QRadar appliance itself. No offense data, event payloads, IP addresses, or usernames are sent to any external service — ever.

This makes QRadar Offense Intelligence deployable in regulated, classified, and air-gapped environments where cloud AI is not permitted.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The AI analysis engine is the core of QRadar Offense Intelligence. It takes a raw QRadar offense and produces a structured, evidence-grounded threat analysis in approximately 60–90 seconds — without sending any data outside the appliance.

The model used is Qwen3.5-9B (Q5 quantized, 6.1 GB), running locally via llama.cpp. No API keys, no cloud connectivity, no data egress.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Analysis runs in five phases, each building on the last:

docs.title: Phase 1 — Rule XML Fetch
docs.text:
The app fetches the full XML definition of every QRadar rule that triggered the offense directly from the QRadar API. The rule XML contains the actual detection conditions — log source filters, threshold counters, reference set checks, network filters — parsed and cleaned before being sent to the model.

This is what allows the AI to answer "why did this rule fire?" with specifics, rather than generic statements.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Event Sampling
docs.text:
Two AQL queries run against QRadar:

  • Offense events — events directly associated with the offense (INOFFENSE query), up to the configured limit
  • Source timeline — all activity from the offense source IP/user in the configured lookback window

Events are deduplicated using QRadar's native coalescing key (QID, sourceIP, destIP, destPort, username) so repeated events are counted rather than listed individually. This keeps the prompt compact and focused.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Historical Context
docs.text:
The app queries its local offense cache to compute:

  • How many times each triggering rule has fired in the past 30 days
  • How many offenses the source has been involved in
  • Whether this offense matches a recurring pattern or is an isolated first occurrence

docs.title: Phase 4 — False Positive Pre-Screening
docs.text:
Before the LLM call, the app checks for known false positive signals:

  • R2R directionality — events where both source and destination are outside the QRadar network hierarchy (strong indicator of a network hierarchy misconfiguration)
  • Management IPs — source IPs in 169.254.x.x or 127.x.x.x ranges
  • Reference set exclusions — rule XML references to exclusion reference sets that may be pending tuning

These signals are injected into the prompt as FALSE POSITIVE CONFIDENCE: HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW so the model's verdict is grounded in pre-computed signals, not just pattern matching.

docs.title: Phase 5 — LLM Inference + Relationship Scoring
docs.text:
The assembled prompt is sent to the local llama.cpp server. The model returns a structured 7-section analysis. After analysis completes, the app computes pairwise relationship scores between this offense and all others in the 30-day window and stores them in the offense_relationships table — used by the Relationship Graph and Campaign Detection.

AI Analysis tab showing the 5-phase pipeline.

docs.title: Analysis Output
docs.text: Each analysis produces seven sections:

docs.title: VERDICT
docs.text:
One of: TRUE POSITIVE | LIKELY FALSE POSITIVE | NEEDS INVESTIGATION

Followed by a one-sentence explanation referencing the specific signals that drove the verdict (IP addresses, rule conditions, recurrence patterns).

docs.title: WHY THIS RULE FIRED
docs.text: A precise explanation of which rule conditions were satisfied, referencing actual IPs, usernames, QIDs, and payload patterns from the sampled events. Derived directly from the rule XML — not inferred.

docs.title: SEVERITY ASSESSMENT
docs.text: A risk assessment grounded in event volume, repeat counts, payload patterns, and the magnitude/severity/credibility scores from QRadar. Explains whether the pattern suggests a genuine threat or misconfiguration noise.

docs.title: LIKELY ATTACK VECTOR
docs.text: The probable attack technique or activity, with specific src/dst pairs and payload samples cited as evidence. Maps to MITRE ATT&CK where applicable.

docs.title: RECOMMENDED IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
docs.text: 3–5 specific, actionable steps naming the actual source IPs, rule names, or reference sets involved. Automatically extracted and saved as response tasks if you click Load AI Tasks.

docs.title: FALSE POSITIVE TUNING
docs.text: If the verdict is false positive: 2–4 specific tuning steps referencing the exact rule name, reference set names, and condition text. If true positive: No tuning recommended — investigate as genuine threat.

docs.title: INVESTIGATION STEPS
docs.text: 3–5 forensic steps referencing the actual IPs, users, and payload patterns in the evidence. These form the basis for the investigation task list.

docs.title: Analysis Queue
docs.text:
The analysis queue is a single-worker queue — one offense is analyzed at a time to prevent resource contention on the LLM.

  • Queue depth is shown in the Analysis Queue panel on any offense's AI tab
  • Position in the queue is shown so analysts know how long to wait
  • Human-triggered analyses take priority — the MITRE Tagger scheduler job yields immediately when a human queues an analysis

To trigger analysis: open any offense → AI Analysis tab → Analyze.

docs.title: Inference Timeout
docs.text:
The default inference timeout is 600 seconds (10 minutes). On slower hardware where token generation is below ~1 token/second, longer analyses may time out.

If you see timed out in the analysis queue, increase the timeout under Settings → System Settings → AI Inference Timeout. A value of 900 seconds (15 minutes) is recommended for CPU-only deployments.

docs.title: Auto-Triage
docs.text:
Auto-triage automatically queues new offenses for AI analysis when they meet configurable thresholds for magnitude and severity. Enable and configure it under Settings → System Settings → Auto-Triage.

Setting Description Enabled Toggle auto-triage on/off Minimum Magnitude Only queue offenses at or above this magnitude (0–10) Minimum Severity Only queue offenses at or above this severity (0–10) Match condition Either (OR) — queue if magnitude OR severity meets threshold. Both (AND) — require both.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Once AI analysis has completed for an offense, click AI Generate in the Executive Summary section of the Overview tab to generate a formal incident report. The summary is structured as a shareable markdown document including verdict, key evidence, risk assessment, recommended actions, and investigation steps.

The summary can be manually edited and saved, or copied to clipboard for sharing with stakeholders.

Info

The AI Generate button is disabled until AI analysis has been run on the offense. Run analysis first from the AI Analysis tab.

docs.title: Event Sampling Configuration
docs.text:
The amount of data fed to the AI can be tuned under Settings → System Settings → AI Event Sampling:

Setting Default Description Offense event limit 10 Max rows from the INOFFENSE AQL query Source event limit 15 Max rows from the source timeline query Offense max window (hours) 24 Cap on the offense event query lookback Source lookback (hours) 24 How far back to search source activity

Increasing these values gives the model more evidence to work with but increases prompt size and inference time.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Analytics dashboard gives SOC managers and team leads visibility into operational performance — how fast the team is detecting and responding, who is carrying what workload, which offenses are at risk of breaching SLA, and where the team is stalling.

Navigate to Analytics in the left navigation bar.

Analytics dashboard — operational metrics, SLA status, and analyst workload at a glance.

docs.title: MTTD — Mean Time to Detect
docs.text: The average time between when an offense first occurred (QRadar start_time) and when it was first acknowledged or assigned. Measures how quickly threats are being seen.

docs.title: MTTR — Mean Time to Respond
docs.text: The average time between offense creation and closure. The primary SOC performance metric — lower is better.

docs.title: MTTA — Mean Time to Acknowledge
docs.text:
The average time between offense creation and when an analyst first acts on it (assignment or lifecycle stage change). A high MTTA indicates offenses are sitting in the queue unattended.

All three metrics are displayed as trend charts over a rolling period, allowing managers to see whether response times are improving or degrading.

docs.title: SLA thresholds
docs.text:
SLA thresholds define the maximum acceptable time to resolve an offense by severity band. Configure them under Settings → System Settings → SLA Thresholds.

Default thresholds:

Severity Default SLA Critical 4 hours High 24 hours Medium 72 hours Low 7 days

docs.title: SLA status per offense
docs.text: Each open offense shows an SLA indicator with: - Time remaining until SLA breach - Percentage consumed of the SLA budget - At-risk status (orange) when the configured at-risk threshold is reached (default: 80% consumed) - Breached status (red) when 100% is consumed

docs.title: SLA notifications
docs.text:
Bell menu — SLA breach and at-risk notifications with per-notification dismissal.

The SLA Breach Checker job (runs daily at 00:00 by default) raises notifications for:

  • At-risk — offense has consumed ≥ the configured at-risk threshold % of its SLA
  • Breach — offense has consumed 100% of its SLA (is overdue)

Notifications appear in the bell menu (top right of the application). The bell shows a badge count of unread notifications.

Each notification can be dismissed individually with a dismissal reason. Dismissed notifications are retained for the configured retention period (default: 7 days) before being purged.

docs.title: Severity Breakdown
docs.text: Pie/donut chart showing the distribution of open offenses by severity band (Critical, High, Medium, Low). A quick check on the overall health of the queue.

docs.title: 14-Day Severity Trend
docs.text: Line chart showing daily offense volume by severity over the past 14 days. Use this to identify whether offense volume is growing, stable, or declining across severity bands.

docs.title: Analyst Workload
docs.text: Bar chart showing the number of open offenses assigned to each analyst. Use this to identify overloaded analysts and redistribute work.

docs.title: Top Attack Sources
docs.text: Ranked list of the most active attacker sources (offense_source values) by number of offenses in the past 30 days. An IP appearing repeatedly here may warrant blocking or escalation.

docs.title: Stalled Cases
docs.text: List of offenses that have not had a lifecycle stage change in longer than a configurable period. These are investigations that have stopped progressing — either blocked, forgotten, or waiting for action.

docs.title: Analyst Capacity
docs.text: Shows the ratio of open high/critical severity offenses per analyst, helping identify when the team needs additional resources.

docs.title: Age Distribution
docs.text: Distribution of open offenses by how long they have been open (e.g. < 1 day, 1–7 days, 7–30 days, > 30 days). A large proportion in the older buckets indicates a backlog.

docs.title: Offense Type Breakdown
docs.text: Distribution of offenses by QRadar offense type. Useful for identifying which offense categories dominate the queue.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text: Configure SLA thresholds by severity under Settings → System Settings → SLA Thresholds. Values are entered in hours and minutes.

docs.title: At-risk threshold
docs.text: The At-risk threshold (%) controls when the orange at-risk notification fires. Default is 80% — meaning when an offense has consumed 80% of its SLA budget, it becomes at-risk. Set this lower (e.g. 60%) for more lead time, or higher (e.g. 90%) to reduce notification noise.

docs.title: Notification retention
docs.text: Dismissed SLA notifications are retained for the configured retention period before being auto-purged. Default is 7 days. Adjust under Settings → System Settings → SLA Notifications.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A sophisticated attacker rarely generates a single offense. They generate dozens — each one looking isolated when viewed individually. Campaign Detection automatically identifies that those offenses are related and surfaces them as a named attack campaign with a unified kill chain, date range, and analyst context.

No AI required

Campaign Detection is pure graph computation — no LLM inference. It works by grouping offenses that share the same detection rule or attacker source, then running a BFS (breadth-first search) to find connected clusters. It is fast, deterministic, and runs even on offenses that have never been AI-analyzed.

docs.title: 1. Build the adjacency graph
docs.text:
The detection engine queries all offenses in the configured time window (default: 90 days) and builds an adjacency graph:

  • Two offenses are connected if they share at least one QRadar detection rule ID
  • Two offenses are also connected if they share the same offense source (attacker IP, username, or CEP)

This is the same signal used by the Relationship Graph — but applied across all offenses simultaneously rather than from a single offense's perspective.

docs.title: 2. BFS connected components
docs.text: A standard BFS algorithm walks the adjacency graph and groups all reachable offenses into connected components. Each component is a candidate campaign.

docs.title: 3. Filter by minimum size
docs.text: Components with fewer than 3 offenses are discarded (configurable). This prevents single-pair relationships from becoming campaigns.

docs.title: 4. Compute campaign attributes
docs.text:
For each remaining component, the engine computes:

Attribute How it's computed Name Deterministic — see Campaign Naming Kill chain Aggregate MITRE tags across all member offenses, deduplicate by tactic, sort by tactic order First seen / Last seen Min/max of member offense start times Common source Offense source if all members share the same one, else null Shared rule IDs Intersection of rule ID sets across all members Severity max Highest severity among members Assigned analysts All unique non-null analyst assignments Is causal chain True if any lateral movement edge exists between members Status active if any member offense is OPEN, else closed

docs.title: 5. Stable campaign IDs
docs.text:
Each campaign gets a stable ID computed as the MD5 hash of its sorted member offense IDs. This means the same cluster of offenses always gets the same campaign ID — across re-runs, nightly jobs, and manual detections.

If the cluster grows (new offense added), the ID changes because the membership changed. This is by design — it signals the campaign has evolved.

docs.title: Campaign Naming
docs.text:
Campaign names are generated deterministically — no LLM required:

Condition Name format All members share the same offense source Source {IP} · {tactic chain} Members share a common detection rule {Rule Name} · {N} offenses MITRE tactic data available {Top Tactic} Campaign · {N} offenses Fallback Campaign · {N} offenses

The tactic chain appended to source-based names shows the first three tactics in the kill chain (e.g. Reconnaissance → Initial Access → Lateral Movement).

docs.title: On demand
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Campaigns in the left navigation
  2. Click Detect Now
  3. Detection runs in the background — the page polls for completion
  4. Results appear within a few seconds for most environments

docs.title: Scheduled (nightly)
docs.text:
The Campaign Detection scheduler job runs nightly at 04:00 by default (after MITRE tagging at 03:00). Enable it under Settings → Job Scheduler.

The job runs silently, updates existing campaigns with new member offenses, creates new campaigns, and marks campaigns as closed when all their member offenses are closed.

docs.title: Campaign List View
docs.text:
Campaign list — each card shows name, offense count, kill chain progression, severity, and date range.

The Campaigns page shows all detected campaigns grouped by status (Active / Closed).

Each campaign card displays:

  • Name — deterministic campaign name
  • Status badge — ACTIVE or CLOSED
  • Offense count — number of member offenses
  • Max severity — highest severity in the campaign
  • Date range — first seen → last seen
  • Assigned analysts — all analysts who have been assigned any member offense
  • Kill chain bar — tactic chips in kill chain order (e.g. [Recon] → [Initial Access] → [Lateral Movement])
  • Lateral movement warning — shown when a causal chain is confirmed between member offenses

Click any campaign card to open the detail view.

docs.title: Campaign Detail View
docs.text:
Campaign detail — full kill chain with technique IDs and counts, plus a searchable member offense table.

The campaign detail view shows:

docs.title: Kill chain progression
docs.text:
A full tactic breakdown showing which techniques were observed at each stage:

[Reconnaissance]     [Initial Access]     [Lateral Movement]
T1595 · 49 offs  →   T1078 · 8 offs   →   T1021 · 3 offs

Each tactic chip links to the relevant ATT&CK technique page.

docs.title: Shared detection rules
docs.text: The list of QRadar rule IDs present in all (or most) member offenses — the common thread that tied the campaign together.

docs.title: Member offenses table
docs.text: A paginated, searchable table of all member offenses with: - Offense ID and description - Start time - Severity and magnitude - Status and lifecycle stage - Assigned analyst - Click to open the offense in the full Offense Detail view

docs.title: Campaign Banner on Offense Detail
docs.text:
Campaign banner on Offense Detail — click to navigate directly to the campaign view.

When an offense is a member of a detected campaign, a green banner appears on the Offense Detail page (Overview tab, below the SLA indicator):

[Campaign icon]  Campaign: Certificate Validation Wave · 49 offenses    View Campaign →

Clicking the banner navigates directly to the campaign detail view.

docs.title: Lateral Movement Detection
docs.text:
If the pre-computed offense_relationships table contains any pairs with is_causal_chain = 1 between campaign members, the campaign is flagged as a causal chain. This means the destination IPs of one offense's events overlap with the source IPs of a subsequent offense — a direct indicator of lateral movement.

Causal chain campaigns show a ⚠ Lateral movement warning on the campaign card.

Causal chain data requirement

Lateral movement detection requires event-level data from the AI analysis pipeline (Phase 5 relationship scoring). Offenses that have not been AI-analyzed will not contribute causal chain edges, though they can still join campaigns through shared rule or source signals.

docs.title: v1.0.0 — May 2026
docs.text: Initial release of QRadar Offense Intelligence.

docs.title: AI Analysis Engine
docs.text:
• On-device Qwen3.5-9B Model — no cloud dependency, zero data egress
  • 5-phase analysis pipeline: rule XML fetch, event sampling, historical correlation, false positive pre-screening, LLM inference
  • Structured 7-section output: Verdict, Why This Rule Fired, Severity Assessment, Likely Attack Vector, Recommended Immediate Actions, False Positive Tuning, Investigation Steps
  • Analysis queue with real-time position tracking and priority for human-triggered jobs
  • AI-generated response tasks extracted from analysis output
  • AI-generated executive summary (incident report) from cached analysis
  • Auto-triage: configurable automatic queuing of new offenses by magnitude/severity threshold
  • Configurable inference timeout (default: 600 seconds)

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK Integration
docs.text:
• Automated technique tagging via on-device LLM, validated against local ATT&CK knowledge base
  • Local ATT&CK database built from STIX 2.1 bundle — works fully offline
  • Per-offense analyst overrides with team knowledge base promotion
  • Category-to-technique mapping management with confidence scoring
  • Kill chain tactic progression bar on offense detail

docs.title: Attack Campaign Detection
docs.text:
• BFS graph clustering of related offenses by shared detection rule or attacker source
  • Deterministic campaign naming (no LLM required)
  • Kill chain progression assembled from MITRE tags across all member offenses
  • Campaign status tracking (active/closed), severity, date range, and analyst assignments
  • Lateral movement detection and causal chain flagging
  • Campaign banner on Offense Detail linking back to the campaign
  • Nightly scheduled detection with on-demand trigger

docs.title: Offense Relationship Graph
docs.text:
• Interactive vis-network graph with physics-based force layout (forceAtlas2Based)
  • Five investigative lenses: Rule Topology, Attacker Topology, Target Topology, Campaign Topology, Lateral Movement
  • Pre-computed pairwise relationship scoring across 5 dimensions (stored in offense_relationships)
  • Composite scoring: shared rules (35%), attacker source (30%), networks (15%), category+time (12%), lateral hop (8%)
  • Auto-recommendation of strongest lens per offense
  • Directed hierarchical layout for lateral movement chains
  • Node detail panel with match reason chips

docs.title: Investigation Workspace
docs.text:
• Collaborative rich-text notes synced back to QRadar offense notes
  • Evidence file attachments (TXT, LOG, CSV, PDF, DOCX, PNG, JPG) with configurable size limit
  • IOC artifact tracking with type categorisation and context field
  • Response task management with completion tracking and audit
  • SOP Template playbooks — define once, apply in one click with automatic offense matching

docs.title: Offense Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
• Structured lifecycle stages: Triage → Investigation → Containment → Closed
  • Offense assignment with QRadar user directory integration
  • Closure reason selection with sync back to QRadar
  • Tamper-evident audit trail for every action (actor, event type, message, timestamp)
  • Global Audit Trail page with cross-offense activity view

docs.title: Analytics & SLA
docs.text:
• MTTD, MTTR, MTTA trend charts
  • SLA thresholds configurable per severity tier (Critical/High/Medium/Low)
  • SLA breach and at-risk notifications in persistent bell menu
  • Individual notification dismissal with reason logging
  • Analyst workload, stalled case, top attack source, severity breakdown, age distribution dashboards
  • Configurable at-risk threshold percentage and notification retention

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
• Built-in job scheduler with configurable daily run times
  • Jobs: Campaign Detection (04:00), MITRE ATT&CK Tagger (03:00), SLA Breach Checker (00:00), Closed Offense Reconciliation (02:00)
  • On-demand job trigger with run history, duration, and summary tracking

docs.title: Performance & Architecture
docs.text:
• Local SQLite cache — offense list and detail load from on-device storage, not live QRadar API calls
  • Carbon Design System (IBM) frontend — dark theme
  • All offense data served via local cache; QRadar API called only for sync, notes write-back, and user list
  • Air-gap capable — MITRE ATT&CK bundle upload, model file manual copy supported

docs.title: Feedback & Contributing
docs.text:
Found a bug? Have a feature idea? Spotted something wrong in the docs? All feedback is tracked publicly on GitHub so the community can follow along and contribute.

Issues tracker: github.com/prabirmeher/qradar-offense-intelligence-platform/issues

Before opening a new issue, use the search bar on the issues page to check whether someone has already reported the same thing. If they have, add a 👍 reaction or a comment with any additional context — it helps prioritise.

docs.title: Reporting a Bug
docs.text:
Use this when the app behaves unexpectedly, produces an error, or a feature isn't working as described in the docs.

Open a bug report

Include in your report:

Field What to write App version Shown in Settings → System Settings → About Steps to reproduce Numbered steps from a clean state Expected behaviour What should have happened Actual behaviour What actually happened Screenshot or log UI screenshot, or relevant lines from app.log Deployment Docker / bare-metal, host OS, CPU/RAM

The more detail you provide, the faster the issue can be diagnosed.

docs.title: Requesting an Enhancement
docs.text:
Use this for new features, improvements to existing features, or UX suggestions.

Open an enhancement request

Include in your request:

  • Use case — describe the SOC workflow or investigation scenario you're trying to improve
  • Current behaviour — what the app does today (if applicable)
  • Desired behaviour — what you'd like it to do instead
  • Priority context — how often does this come up? Is it a blocker or a nice-to-have?

Enhancement requests are reviewed periodically and tagged for upcoming versions. Popular requests with clear use cases are prioritised.

docs.title: Documentation Correction
docs.text:
Use this when a page is inaccurate, out of date, missing a step, or unclear.

Open a doc correction

Include in your report:

  • Page — the title or URL of the docs page
  • Section — the heading or paragraph that's wrong
  • What's incorrect — what the docs currently say
  • What it should say — the correct information (if you know it)

Documentation corrections are usually quick to fix and are very welcome — even small typos or broken links are worth reporting.

docs.title: Response Times
docs.text:
This is a community-maintained project. There are no guaranteed SLAs for issue responses, but the tracker is checked regularly. Issues are labelled and triaged as:

  • bug — confirmed defects
  • enhancement — accepted feature requests
  • documentation — docs fixes
  • wontfix — out of scope or by design
  • duplicate — already tracked elsewhere

If your issue has been open for a while without a response, feel free to add a comment with any new information — it bumps the issue and helps.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Dashboard is the landing page of QRadar Offense Intelligence. It gives analysts and SOC managers an immediate read on queue health, recent offense activity, and team actions — without navigating anywhere.

Dashboard — stat cards, latest offenses, and the real-time activity feed.

docs.title: Stat Cards
docs.text:
Four summary cards run across the top of the Dashboard:

Card What it shows Open Offenses Total number of open offenses currently in the local cache Unassigned Open offenses with no analyst assigned — a direct signal of queue backlog requiring immediate attention New (24H) Offenses first seen in the last 24 hours, with a trend indicator vs the prior 24-hour period (e.g. ↓ 50% vs prev 24h shown in green when improving, red when worsening) Avg Dwell Time Average age of all open offenses — how long offenses have been sitting unresolved (e.g. 20.7d)

Reading the cards:

  • A high Unassigned count relative to Open Offenses means most of the queue has no owner — triage is not keeping up.
  • A rising Avg Dwell Time means offenses are accumulating faster than they are being closed.
  • New (24H) with an upward trend signals an increase in incoming offense volume that may require staffing attention.

docs.title: Latest Offenses
docs.text:
The Latest Offenses panel shows the most recently created open offenses. Each row includes:

Column Description ID QRadar offense ID — click to open the Offense Detail page Description Offense description from QRadar Created Timestamp when the offense was first seen Severity Color-coded severity label (High, Medium, Low) Assigned Assigned analyst — shown in orange if unassigned SLA Dot indicator: green (within SLA), yellow (at-risk), red (breached) Stage Current lifecycle stage badge (Triage, Investigation, Containment) — blank if not yet progressed

Click View All → to go to the full Offense List.

docs.title: Recent Activity
docs.text:
The Recent Activity panel shows a live feed of analyst actions across all offenses, in reverse chronological order. Each entry shows:

  • Timestamp — when the action occurred
  • Offense link — the offense ID (clickable)
  • Actor — the analyst who performed the action (bold)
  • Action description — what was done (e.g. Advanced offense to Investigation, Logged IP indicator: 8.8.8.8, Loaded SOP: Certificate Validation Passed)

This feed is pulled from the audit trail and reflects all activity: lifecycle stage changes, note additions, artifact logging, SOP loads, task completions, and AI analysis triggers.

Click View All → to open the global Audit Trail page.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Detail IBM QRadar 7.5.0 UP12 and later App container memory 8 GB minimum Network Outbound internet not required after installation but it needs internet during initial setup QRadar user role ADMIN capability required

Memory Requirement

The app requires 8 GB of memory allocated to the QRadar app container. This is set in manifest.json and enforced by the QRadar app framework.

docs.title: Step 1 — Obtain the package
docs.text: Download the latest .zip package from the IBM Application Exchange page.

docs.title: Step 2 — Install via Extensions Management
docs.text:
1. Log in to QRadar as an admin
  2. Navigate to Admin → Extensions Management
  3. Click Add and upload the .zip file
  4. Click Install and confirm

QRadar will deploy the app container. This may take 2–5 minutes on first install as the container image is extracted.

docs.title: Step 3 — Open the app
docs.text: Once installed, the app appears in the QRadar navigation as Offense Intelligence Platform.

docs.title: 1. Configure the QRadar connection
docs.text:
On first launch, you will be redirected to Settings → QRadar Connection.

Enter your QRadar API service token. This token is used to fetch offenses, events, rules, and user lists from QRadar.

Creating a service token

In QRadar: Admin → Authorized Services → Add Authorized Service. Assign the ADMIN role and copy the token.

Click Save, then Test Connection to verify.

docs.title: 2. Download the AI model
docs.text:
Navigate to Model Management (accessible from the top navigation bar).

Click Download Model. The app will download the Qwen3.5-9B Q5 model (~6.1 GB) from Hugging Face directly to the QRadar appliance.

Air-gapped environments

If your QRadar appliance has no outbound internet access, transfer the model file manually to /opt/app-root/store/models/ inside the app container, then click Refresh on the Model Management page.

Once the status shows AI Ready (green dot in the top bar), the platform is fully operational.

Model Management — download progress and AI Ready status indicator.

docs.title: 3. Open the Dashboard
docs.text:
Navigate to Dashboard. The app automatically syncs open offenses from QRadar on the first page load and continues polling in the background every 5 minutes (configurable under Settings → System Settings → Poll Interval).

No manual sync step is required — offenses will appear within seconds of the first load.

Manual refresh

If you want to force an immediate sync at any time, click Sync Now on the Offenses page. This bypasses the poll interval and fetches the latest offenses from QRadar immediately.

Offense list — automatically populated from QRadar on first load.

docs.title: 4. Build the MITRE ATT&CK database
docs.text:
Navigate to Settings → MITRE ATT&CK and click Build Database. This downloads the current ATT&CK framework from MITRE and builds the local knowledge base used for technique validation.

Air-gapped environments

Download the STIX 2.1 bundle from MITRE ATT&CK on a connected machine, then upload it via the Upload Bundle option.

docs.title: Running Your First AI Analysis
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Offenses and open any offense
  2. Click the AI Analysis tab
  3. Click Analyze — the offense is queued for analysis
  4. Watch the Analysis Queue panel (top right of the AI tab) — the job will show as running
  5. Analysis typically completes in 2–10 minutes depending on the appliance hardware and the number of events in the offense. The model runs entirely on the appliance CPU — no GPU or external service is required.

The result includes: verdict, attack narrative, MITRE technique mapping, affected assets, recommended immediate actions, false positive assessment, and investigation steps.

AI analysis result — structured 7-section output with verdict, attack narrative, and recommended actions.

docs.title: Scheduler Jobs
docs.text:
The platform includes a built-in job scheduler that runs nightly tasks automatically. After initial setup, navigate to Settings → Job Scheduler and review the default job schedule:

Job Default time Purpose SLA Breach Checker 00:00 Raises SLA breach and at-risk notifications MITRE ATT&CK Tagger 03:00 Tags AI-analyzed offenses with ATT&CK techniques Campaign Detection 04:00 Clusters related offenses into attack campaigns Closed Offense Reconciliation 02:00 Syncs closed/inactive offenses from QRadar

Enable the jobs you want and adjust the run times to suit your maintenance window.

Job Scheduler — configure run times and monitor last run status for each job.

docs.title: Investigation Workspace
docs.text:
Every offense has a dedicated investigation workspace that combines all the context an analyst needs — notes, evidence files, IOCs, tasks, and playbooks — without leaving QRadar.

The workspace is organized into tabs on the Offense Detail page: Overview, AI Analysis, Notes, Files, Artifacts, Tasks, and Related.

Investigation workspace — all tabs for a single offense: Notes, Files, Artifacts, Tasks, and Related offenses.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The Notes tab provides a rich-text collaboration space for investigation notes.

  • Notes support full rich-text formatting (bold, italic, lists, code blocks)
  • Each note records the author and timestamp
  • Notes written here are synced back to QRadar as offense notes, so they appear in the native QRadar offense view as well
  • Multiple analysts can add notes — all notes are visible to the whole team

docs.title: Writing a note
docs.text:
1. Open the Notes tab on any offense
  2. Type in the note editor
  3. Click Add Note — the note is saved and synced to QRadar

docs.title: Files (Attachments)
docs.text:
The Files tab allows analysts to upload and manage evidence files tied to the offense.

Supported file types: TXT, LOG, CSV, PDF, DOCX, PNG, JPG

Supported operations: - Upload one or more files (up to the configured size limit per file) - Download any attachment - Delete attachments you no longer need

Each attachment records the filename, file size, MIME type, uploader, and upload timestamp.

docs.title: Configuring the size limit
docs.text: Maximum attachment size is configurable under Settings → System Settings → Attachments (default: 5 MB, max: 50 MB).

docs.title: Artifacts (IOC Tracking)
docs.text:
The Artifacts tab is an indicator of compromise (IOC) tracker. Use it to log any observable that is relevant to the investigation.

Artifact types: - ip — IP address - domain — domain name - hash — file hash (MD5, SHA1, SHA256) - url — URL - user — username or account - email — email address - other — any other observable

Each artifact has: - Type — the category above - Value — the actual indicator - Context — free-text field describing why this indicator is relevant (e.g. "C2 beacon destination observed in events", "Lateral movement credential") - Created by and timestamp

Artifacts are stored locally and tied to the offense. They are not synced to QRadar.

docs.title: Response Tasks
docs.text: The Tasks tab provides a structured checklist for tracking investigation and response steps.

docs.title: Manual tasks
docs.text: Click Add Task to create a task with a free-text description. Tasks can be marked as done, with the completion time and analyst recorded.

docs.title: AI-generated tasks
docs.text:
After AI analysis has run on an offense, click Load AI Tasks to extract the recommended actions directly from the analysis output. Three categories of tasks are imported:

Prefix Source section [Immediate] Recommended Immediate Actions [Investigation] Investigation Steps [Tuning] False Positive Tuning

docs.title: SOP Playbook tasks
docs.text:
Standard Operating Procedure templates can be applied in one click. When a matching SOP template exists for the offense type or name pattern, a Load SOP button appears. Clicking it imports the full SOP task list.

See SOP Templates below for how to create and manage templates.

docs.title: Task tracking
docs.text:
• Each task shows created time and completion status
  • Completed tasks show who completed them and when
  • Tasks are sorted: incomplete first, completed below

Response Tasks — AI-generated tasks prefixed with [Immediate], [Investigation], [Tuning] alongside manual tasks.

docs.title: SOP Templates
docs.text: SOP Templates are reusable playbooks that define a standard set of investigation tasks for a given offense type or name pattern. They are managed under Settings → SOP Templates.

docs.title: Creating a template
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Settings → SOP Templates
  2. Click New Template
  3. Fill in:
  4. Name — descriptive name for the template (e.g. "Brute Force Response")
  5. Offense Type — optional: match by QRadar offense type (numeric ID)
  6. Name Pattern — optional: match by offense description containing this text (case-insensitive)
  7. Tasks — add one task per line
  8. Click Save

docs.title: How matching works
docs.text:
When you open an offense and click Load SOP, the app checks all templates and offers any that match:

  • If offense_type is set and matches the offense's type → match
  • If name_pattern is set and the offense description contains the pattern → match
  • Multiple templates can match — you select which one to apply

docs.title: Example templates
docs.text:
Brute Force 

- Block source IP at perimeter firewall
- Check authentication logs for successful logins from source
- Review all accounts the source attempted to authenticate to
- Reset passwords for any accounts that successfully authenticated
- Escalate if lateral movement detected

Certificate Validation 

- Identify all destination IPs in the offense events
- Verify certificate validity for each destination
- Check if source is a known scanner or pen test tool
- Review QRadar network hierarchy — confirm source is correctly classified
- If legitimate traffic: tune the rule to exclude this source/destination pair

docs.title: Audit Trail
docs.text:
Every action taken on every offense is recorded in a tamper-evident audit trail:

  • Note added / edited
  • File uploaded / deleted
  • Artifact added / deleted
  • Task created / completed
  • Lifecycle stage changed
  • Assignment changed
  • AI analysis triggered / completed
  • Offense closed / reopened

The audit trail records the actor (QRadar username), event type, message, and timestamp. It is visible on the offense detail page and in the global Audit Trail page (showing activity across all offenses).

Retention is configurable under Settings → System Settings → Audit Trail (default: 90 days, minimum: 30 days). Open offense audit trails are never purged regardless of age.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: QRadar Offense Intelligence adds a structured lifecycle to every offense, tracking it from initial triage through investigation, containment, and closure. Every stage change, assignment, and closure is recorded in the audit trail with the analyst's name and timestamp.

docs.title: Lifecycle Stages
docs.text:
Lifecycle stepper on Offense Detail — click any stage to advance the offense.

Triage → Investigation → Containment → Closed
Stage Meaning Triage New offense — analyst is determining if it's real and how urgent it is Investigation Confirmed as real (or needs deeper analysis) — active investigation underway Containment Root cause identified — containment/remediation actions in progress Closed Resolved — offense closed with a reason

Stages are displayed as a stepper at the top of each Offense Detail page. Click any stage to advance or move the offense to that stage.

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
Offenses can be assigned to any QRadar analyst. The assigned analyst is shown in the offense overview and in the Analytics workload view.

To assign an offense: 1. Open the offense 2. Click the Assigned To field 3. Select an analyst from the QRadar user list

The assignment is recorded in the audit trail and written back to QRadar.

docs.title: Closing an Offense
docs.text:
To close an offense, advance its lifecycle stage to Closed. You will be prompted to select a closing reason:

Reason When to use False Positive The offense was triggered by benign activity Resolved The threat was identified and remediated Duplicate This offense is a duplicate of another No Action Required The activity is known-good and no action was needed Other Any other reason

The closing reason and the closing analyst are recorded in the audit trail and synced to QRadar.

docs.title: Pending QRadar close
docs.text: When an offense is closed in QRadar Offense Intelligence, a pending_qradar_close flag is set. The Closed Offense Reconciliation scheduler job processes these and closes the offense in QRadar itself, ensuring both systems stay in sync.

docs.title: Audit Trail
docs.text:
Global Audit Trail — every action across all offenses with actor, event type, and timestamp.

The audit trail records every action taken on every offense. It is visible:

  • Per offense — on the Offense Detail page (scroll to the bottom of any tab)
  • Globally — on the Audit Trail page (left navigation)

Each entry includes:

Field Description Actor QRadar username of the analyst who performed the action Event type Category of action (e.g. lifecycle_change, note_added, task_completed) Message Human-readable description of what happened Timestamp UTC timestamp of the action

docs.title: Audit trail retention
docs.text: By default, audit trail entries for closed or purged offenses are retained for 90 days before being purged. Open offense audit trails are never purged. Configure the retention period under Settings → System Settings → Audit Trail.

docs.title: QRadar Synchronisation
docs.text:
QRadar Offense Intelligence maintains a local cache of offense data for performance. Changes made in the platform are synced back to QRadar:

Action Sync behaviour Add note Written to QRadar offense notes immediately Assign offense Written to QRadar assigned user field Close offense Sets pending_qradar_close flag; processed by Closed Offense Reconciliation job Lifecycle stage change Stored locally only (QRadar has no native lifecycle stage concept)

The Closed Offense Reconciliation job also syncs in the other direction — picking up offenses that were closed or made inactive in QRadar and updating their status in the local cache.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
QRadar Offense Intelligence integrates the MITRE ATT&CK framework at two levels:

  1. Per-offense technique tagging — the on-device LLM identifies which ATT&CK techniques apply to each analyzed offense, validated against a local ATT&CK knowledge base
  2. Campaign kill chain — technique tags across member offenses are aggregated into a kill chain progression visible on the Campaigns page

All ATT&CK data is stored and processed locally. No external lookups are made at query time.

docs.title: Building the ATT&CK Database
docs.text: Before technique tagging can run, you must build the local ATT&CK knowledge base.

docs.title: Connected environments
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Settings → MITRE ATT&CK
  2. Click Build Database
  3. The app downloads the current ATT&CK STIX 2.1 bundle from MITRE and parses it into the local database

This takes approximately 30–60 seconds. The database version and build date are shown after completion.

docs.title: Air-gapped environments
docs.text:
1. On a connected machine, download the ATT&CK STIX 2.1 bundle from https://attack.mitre.org/ (Enterprise ATT&CK JSON)
  2. Transfer the file to a machine that can reach the QRadar web interface
  3. Navigate to Settings → MITRE ATT&CK → Upload Bundle
  4. Select the downloaded JSON file and click Upload

docs.title: Automatic Technique Tagging
docs.text:
The MITRE ATT&CK Tagger is a scheduler job that runs nightly (default: 03:00) and tags all AI-analyzed offenses that have not yet been tagged.

For each offense, the tagger:

  1. Sends the offense description, categories, and AI analysis verdict to the on-device LLM
  2. Asks it to identify the most applicable ATT&CK techniques
  3. Validates each returned technique ID against the local knowledge base — invalid or hallucinated IDs are corrected or discarded
  4. Writes results to the offense_mitre_tags table with technique ID, name, tactic, tactic order, confidence score, and reasoning

The tagger yields immediately if a human-triggered analysis is queued — it never competes with analyst-initiated work.

docs.title: Triggering manually
docs.text:
To run the tagger on demand: Settings → Job Scheduler → MITRE ATT&CK Tagger → Run Now.

MITRE ATT&CK settings — database version, category-to-technique mappings, and upload option for air-gapped environments.

docs.title: Viewing Technique Tags on an Offense
docs.text:
Technique tags appear as tactic chips in two places:

  • Offense Detail → Overview tab — a kill chain bar showing the tactic progression for this offense
  • Offense Detail → AI Analysis tab — technique tags listed alongside the analysis

Each chip shows the tactic name and technique ID (e.g. T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter). Hovering shows the full technique name and confidence score.

Kill chain bar on Offense Detail — tactic chips in ATT&CK order with technique IDs.

docs.title: Analyst Overrides
docs.text:
If the AI-assigned technique is incorrect, analysts can override it.

  1. On the Offense Detail page, click Edit MITRE Tags (pencil icon next to the kill chain bar)
  2. Search for the correct technique by name or ID
  3. Select it — the override replaces the AI tag for this offense
  4. Optionally click Promote to Knowledge Base to share the mapping with the team

docs.title: How overrides work
docs.text: Overrides are stored in a separate offense_mitre_overrides table and take precedence over AI tags in all views. The original AI tag is preserved and can be restored if needed.

docs.title: Category Mappings
docs.text:
The Category Mappings section under Settings → MITRE ATT&CK shows the team's shared knowledge base: a mapping of QRadar event categories to ATT&CK techniques.

These mappings are: - Populated automatically when analysts promote verified override mappings - Used by the tagger as additional context when tagging offenses with those categories - Editable by any analyst — you can add, update, or remove mappings

Column Description Category QRadar event category name Technique ID ATT&CK technique (e.g. T1078) Technique Name Human-readable technique name Tactic ATT&CK tactic Confidence 0.0–1.0 confidence score Verified Whether a human analyst has verified this mapping

docs.title: Tactic Order Reference
docs.text:
Tactics are ordered by ATT&CK kill chain stage. This order is used to sort the kill chain bar and campaign tactic progression:

Order Tactic 1 Reconnaissance 2 Resource Development 3 Initial Access 4 Execution 5 Persistence 6 Privilege Escalation 7 Defense Evasion 8 Credential Access 9 Discovery 10 Lateral Movement 11 Collection 12 Command and Control 13 Exfiltration 14 Impact

docs.title: Slide Deck Outline for CISO · CTO · Product Leadership
docs.text: Format: Copy each slide's content into PowerPoint or Google Slides. Timing guide: Each slide shows its target duration in (italics). Speaker notes are below each slide's bullet points. Suggested visual is noted at the end of each slide.

docs.title: SLIDE 1 — Title Slide (0:30)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: AI-Powered SOC Investigation — On-Device · Zero Data Egress
docs.text:
Sub-line:

Structured threat analysis in 90 seconds. No cloud. No egress. No compromise.

Your name · Date · Confidential

Speaker notes:

"Today I'm going to show you something I've been building by looking hard at the real friction points SOC analysts face every day with QRadar — and asking: what if the AI did the hard part, but never left the building?"

Visual: Full-bleed screenshot of the Offense Detail page (hero-offense-detail.png) with a dark overlay behind the title text.

docs.title: SLIDE 2 — The Problem: SOC Triage is a Human Bottleneck (2:00)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Every QRadar offense is a question that needs an answer
docs.text:
Bullets: - QRadar surfaces raw metadata: rule names, source IPs, event counts - Turning that into a verdict requires an analyst to manually query events, read rule XML, consult runbooks, and cross-reference history - At scale: 30 minutes to several hours per offense - The analyst is the bottleneck — not the detection engine

The metric that matters:

Mean Time to Respond (MTTR) is driven by triage time, not detection time.

Speaker notes:

"QRadar is excellent at detecting. The problem starts the moment an offense appears in the queue. The analyst opens it and sees a rule name and an IP address. What they need is a verdict — is this real? What happened? What do I do next? Getting there today is a completely manual process. Let me show you what that costs."

Visual: A simple two-column diagram — left: "What QRadar gives you" (rule name, IP, event count) → right: "What you need to act" (verdict, kill chain, recommended actions). Red arrow showing the manual gap.

docs.title: SLIDE 3 — The Status Quo at Scale (1:30)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: The math doesn't work at scale
docs.text:
Data points (use large typography): - 30–120 min average triage time per offense - Dozens to hundreds of offenses per day in a mature SOC - 1 analyst can only deeply investigate 4–8 offenses per shift - Result: a growing backlog of uninvestigated alerts

The real cost:

Alert fatigue → analysts skip investigation → threats are missed. Backlog → SLA breaches → compliance risk.

Speaker notes:

"This isn't a hypothetical. Any SOC running QRadar at scale lives with this. The queue grows faster than analysts can work through it. And when analysts are overwhelmed, they start closing things without investigating — which is exactly the behavior that lets real threats slip through."

Visual: A simple queue diagram — offenses piling up on the left, one analyst on the right. Red "SLA breach" label on the oldest offenses.

docs.title: SLIDE 4 — Why Existing AI Solutions Don't Solve It (2:00)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Cloud AI is blocked by the data you can't share
docs.text:
The three blockers: 1. Data egress — offense events contain IPs, usernames, payloads. Sending them to a cloud API violates data residency laws, classified environment policies, and customer data agreements. 2. Air-gapped environments — government, financial, healthcare customers can't reach external APIs at all. 3. Vendor lock-in & cost — pay-per-token pricing on hundreds of offenses per day adds up fast.

The result:

Security teams that most need AI assistance are the ones least able to use it.

Speaker notes:

"The obvious answer is 'use an LLM API.' But the moment you do that, you're sending your offense events — your source IPs, your usernames, your event payloads — to a third-party server. That's a non-starter for regulated industries. For classified environments, it's simply not possible. I built this with that constraint as a first principle, not an afterthought."

Visual: A diagram showing the cloud AI data flow with a red "BLOCKED" symbol. Then a second diagram showing on-device inference with a green "COMPLIANT" label.

docs.title: SLIDE 5 — Introducing QRadar Offense Intelligence (1:30)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: The intelligence layer QRadar was always missing
docs.text:
What it is:

A native QRadar application that embeds an on-device AI analysis engine, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, attack campaign detection, and a full investigation workspace — entirely within the QRadar appliance.

Six capabilities in one platform: 1. On-Device AI Analysis (Qwen3.5-9B · llama.cpp) 2. MITRE ATT&CK Automatic Technique Tagging 3. Attack Campaign Detection 4. Interactive Relationship Graph 5. Investigation Workspace (Notes · IOCs · Tasks · Playbooks) 6. SLA Management & Analytics

The constraint it was built for:

Zero data egress. Everything runs on the QRadar appliance itself.

Speaker notes:

"Let me walk you through what I built. Six integrated capabilities. One platform. And the LLM never makes a network call."

Visual: A clean product overview diagram — QRadar appliance box containing the six capability icons in a honeycomb or grid layout.

docs.title: SLIDE 6 — How It Works: Architecture in One Slide (2:00)
docs.text:
[For CTO / Engineering audience — can go deeper in Q&A]

Headline:

docs.title: Local LLM inference on the QRadar appliance
docs.text:
Architecture diagram components:

QRadar SIEM
    │
    ├── QRadar REST API ──► Rule XML fetch
    │                  ──► AQL event queries
    │                  ──► Offense sync
    │
    └── QRadar App Container (8 GB)
            │
            ├── Flask backend (Python)
            │       ├── 5-phase analysis pipeline
            │       ├── Campaign detection (BFS graph)
            │       ├── Relationship scoring engine
            │       └── Job scheduler
            │
            ├── llama.cpp server
            │       └── Qwen3.5-9B Q5 (6.1 GB, on-device)
            │
            ├── SQLite local database
            │       ├── offense cache + relationships
            │       ├── MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base
            │       └── investigation workspace data
            │
            └── React frontend

Key engineering decisions: - Qwen3.5-9B Q5 — 6.1 GB quantized model, strong instruction following, fits in 8 GB container - llama.cpp — zero-dependency inference, runs on CPU without GPU - SQLite — no external database, no config, survives appliance restarts - BFS campaign detection — deterministic, no LLM needed, runs in seconds - Pre-computed relationship scores — graph renders instantly at query time

Speaker notes:

"The model runs in llama.cpp directly in the app container. No separate inference server, no GPU required. The entire analysis pipeline — rule XML parsing, event sampling, historical context, false positive signals, LLM inference — runs in under two minutes. For the campaign detection engine I deliberately avoided using the LLM — it's pure graph computation with BFS, which means it's fast, deterministic, and free to run as often as you want."

Visual: The architecture diagram above, rendered cleanly.

docs.title: SLIDE 7 — Feature: On-Device AI Analysis (3:00)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: A structured verdict in 90 seconds — without sending data anywhere
docs.text:
The 5-phase pipeline:

Phase What happens 1. Rule XML Fetch Pulls the full detection rule XML from QRadar API — the actual conditions that fired 2. Event Sampling AQL queries for offense events + source IP timeline (deduplicated) 3. Historical Context Rule fire frequency, source offense history from local cache 4. FP Pre-screening R2R directionality, management IPs, reference set exclusions — pre-computed signals 5. LLM Inference Structured prompt → Qwen3.5-9B → 7-section analysis

The 7-section output every analyst gets: - VERDICT — True Positive / Likely False Positive / Needs Investigation - Why This Rule Fired — specific rule conditions and signals, not generic text - Severity Assessment — grounded in event volume, magnitude, credibility - Likely Attack Vector — technique + evidence citations - Recommended Immediate Actions — 3–5 specific steps (auto-loaded as response tasks) - False Positive Tuning — exact rule and reference set names to tune - Investigation Steps — forensic steps citing actual IPs, users, payloads

The number that matters:

90 seconds vs. 30–120 minutes of manual analysis.

Speaker notes:

"The key insight is in Phase 1. Most LLM security tools send the offense description to the model and ask it to guess what happened. We pull the full rule XML — the actual detection logic — and inject it. That's why the output says things like 'this rule fired because the source IP matched reference set XYZ on port 443' instead of 'this appears to be suspicious traffic.' The model has the evidence. It's not guessing."

Visual: Screenshot of ai-analysis-result.png and ai-analysis-queue.png side by side.

docs.title: SLIDE 8 — Feature: MITRE ATT&CK Mapping (2:00)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Every offense tagged to the kill chain — automatically
docs.text:
How it works: - Nightly scheduled job sends offense + AI verdict to the on-device LLM - Model returns ATT&CK technique IDs - Each ID is validated against a local ATT&CK knowledge base — hallucinated IDs are discarded - Results stored with technique name, tactic, confidence score, and reasoning

Analyst controls: - Override any AI-assigned technique with the correct one - Promote verified mappings to a shared team knowledge base — QRadar category → ATT&CK technique - Shared mappings improve future auto-tagging for the whole team

Air-gap support: - ATT&CK bundle can be uploaded manually — no internet access required at tagging time

Visual:

Kill chain bar on offense detail: [Reconnaissance T1595] → [Initial Access T1078] → [Lateral Movement T1021]

Speaker notes:

"Because every offense is tagged, when you look at a campaign you get the aggregate kill chain across all member offenses. You can see at a glance: this attacker started with reconnaissance, got initial access through valid accounts, and is now moving laterally. That context used to require an analyst to manually correlate. Now it's automatic."

Visual: Screenshot of mitre-kill-chain.png.

docs.title: SLIDE 9 — Feature: Attack Campaign Detection (2:00)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Sophisticated attackers generate many offenses. We connect them.
docs.text:
The problem it solves:

A persistent attacker generates 40 offenses over two weeks — each one looking isolated when viewed alone. Campaign Detection finds the pattern.

How detection works: 1. Build an adjacency graph: offenses connected by shared detection rules OR shared attacker source 2. BFS walk finds connected components — clusters of related offenses 3. Filter: minimum 3 offenses to form a campaign 4. Compute: kill chain progression, severity, analyst assignments, lateral movement flags

What you see: - Named campaign with kill chain progression bar - [Recon] → [Initial Access] → [Lateral Movement] - ⚠ Lateral movement warning when hop chains are confirmed - All member offenses linked in one view

Key property:

Pure graph computation — no LLM. Fast, deterministic, runs nightly automatically.

Speaker notes:

"This is one of my favorite parts of the platform. Campaign detection doesn't need the LLM at all. It's a BFS on a graph where edges represent shared rules or shared attacker sources. It runs in seconds and it finds patterns that are genuinely invisible when you're looking at one offense at a time. The lateral movement detection is particularly powerful — it compares the destination IPs of one offense's events against the source IPs of the next offense, which is a direct signal of a hop chain."

Visual: Screenshot of campaigns-list.png and campaign-detail.png.

docs.title: SLIDE 10 — Feature: Relationship Graph (2:00)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Five investigative lenses on how offenses connect
docs.text:
The five lenses:

Lens The question it answers Rule Topology Which other offenses share the same detection rules? Attacker Topology What else has this attacker done in the environment? Target Topology What other offenses targeted the same network segment? Campaign Topology Which offenses share categories in the same time window? Lateral Movement Is there a directed hop chain — has the attacker moved?

Engineering note:

Graph data is pre-computed during AI analysis and stored. Rendering is instant at query time — no computation on graph load.

Smart recommendations:

When you open the graph, the platform recommends the strongest lens for that offense automatically.

Speaker notes:

"Every analyst has looked at an offense and wondered 'what else should I be looking at?' The relationship graph answers that question visually. The lateral movement lens is the most operationally significant — it's a directed timeline showing you exactly which IP hopped from which offense to the next. You can trace an attacker's path through the environment."

Visual: Screenshot of relationship-graph-rule.png and relationship-graph-lateral.png.

docs.title: SLIDE 11 — Feature: Investigation Workspace (1:30)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Everything an analyst needs — without leaving QRadar
docs.text:
What's inside every offense:

Tab What it provides Notes Rich-text collaborative notes — synced back to QRadar offense notes Files Evidence attachments (logs, screenshots, PDFs) tied to the offense Artifacts IOC tracker: IPs, domains, hashes, URLs, users, emails Tasks AI-generated tasks + SOP playbook templates + manual checklist Audit Trail Every action, every actor, every timestamp — tamper-evident

AI-generated response tasks:

After AI analysis, one click loads categorized tasks: [Immediate] · [Investigation] · [Tuning]

SOP Playbooks:

Define templates per offense type or name pattern — load the full playbook in one click.

Speaker notes:

"This replaces the spreadsheets, the shared OneNote, the Slack threads, the email chains that analysts use today to track investigations. Everything is bound to the offense, attributed to the analyst, and timestamped. The audit trail alone has compliance value — every CISO I've spoken to has asked 'how do we prove what we did and when?'"

Visual: Screenshot of investigation-workspace.png and response-tasks.png.

docs.title: SLIDE 12 — Feature: SLA Management & Analytics (1:30)
docs.text: Headline:

docs.title: Visibility into team performance — and early warning before breaches
docs.text:
Operational metrics tracked: - MTTD — Mean Time to Detect (time from offense start to first analyst action) - MTTR — Mean Time to Respond (offense creation to closure) - MTTA — Mean Time to Acknowledge (creation to first assignment)

docs.title: Appendix A — Detailed Technical Q&A Prep
docs.text:
Q: Why Qwen3.5-9B and not a larger model?

9B parameters at Q5 quantization is 6.1 GB — it fits in the 8 GB container allocation with headroom. It produces quality analysis in 60–90 seconds on CPU. A larger model (e.g. 70B) would require 20–40 GB and take 10–20 minutes per inference, making the analyst experience unacceptable. Qwen3.5 specifically was chosen for strong instruction following and structured output compliance.

Q: What happens if the LLM produces a wrong verdict?

The verdict is a recommendation, not an automated action — the analyst makes the final call. False positive pre-screening (Phase 4) grounds the verdict in pre-computed signals so the model isn't making unsupported claims. Analyst override is always available. In practice, the value is in the 90-second analysis vs. 30-minute manual triage — even an imperfect AI verdict that directs investigation correctly is a massive throughput improvement.

Q: How are campaign IDs stable across re-runs?

Campaign ID is the MD5 hash of the sorted set of member offense IDs. Same members = same ID. If a new offense joins the cluster, the ID changes — by design, signaling the campaign has evolved. This makes campaigns trackable in reporting systems and safe to use as foreign keys.

Q: What is the inference timeout and can it be tuned?

Default is 600 seconds. On slower hardware (older QRadar appliances with fewer CPU cores), token generation may be under 1 token/second. The timeout is configurable under Settings → System Settings → AI Inference Timeout. 900 seconds is recommended for CPU-only deployments on constrained hardware.

Q: Does this work on multi-host QRadar deployments?

The app container runs on the QRadar Console. AQL queries and rule XML fetches go through the standard QRadar API, which handles multi-host event routing transparently. The app doesn't need to be aware of managed host topology.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Relationship Graph is an interactive network visualisation that shows how a specific offense relates to others in your environment. It answers the question: "What else should I be looking at while investigating this offense?"

Access it from any Offense Detail page by clicking View Connections (in the Historical Pattern strip).

Relationship Graph — Rule Topology lens. Purple diamonds are rule hubs; offense nodes color-coded by magnitude.

docs.title: Five Investigative Lenses
docs.text: The graph offers five switchable lenses, each answering a different investigative question. You can switch lenses at any time using the View as dropdown in the top bar.

docs.title: Rule Topology
docs.text:
Question: Which other offenses share the same detection rules?

Hub nodes (purple diamonds) represent QRadar detection rules. Offense nodes connect to the rule hubs they triggered. The hub size scales with the number of offenses that have triggered that rule — a large hub indicates a frequently-firing rule, which may signal either a high-activity threat actor or a candidate for rule tuning.

Source hubs (colored boxes) are also shown when the offense source has triggered multiple offenses. The color of the source hub indicates the source type: - Yellow — IP address - Green — Username - Teal — Custom Event Property (CEP)

docs.title: Attacker Topology
docs.text:
Question: What else has this attacker done?

Groups related offenses by their offense source (attacker IP, username, or CEP). Each unique source gets its own hub node. If the attacker has been involved in multiple offenses, all of them are connected through their shared source hub — giving a complete picture of attacker activity in the environment.

docs.title: Target Topology
docs.text:
Question: What other offenses targeted the same network?

Groups offenses by shared destination networks (from QRadar's network hierarchy). Useful for identifying whether a campaign is targeting a specific network segment, a VLAN, or a business unit's infrastructure.

docs.title: Campaign Topology
docs.text:
Question: Which offenses share the same attack category and time window?

Groups offenses sharing the same QRadar event categories, weighted by temporal proximity. Edges include a time delta label (e.g. Δ2.3h) showing how close in time the offenses occurred. Campaign topology is strongest when offenses share categories and occurred within hours of each other.

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Question: Is there a directed hop chain between these offenses?

Lateral Movement lens — directed timeline showing hop chain. Orange arrows indicate dest IP → source IP overlap.

The only directed lens. Renders a left-to-right timeline showing offense nodes sorted by start time, with directed orange arrows between offenses where a lateral hop was detected — meaning the destination IPs of one offense's events overlap with the source IPs of the next offense.

This lens uses event-level data from the AI analysis pipeline and is available only for offenses that have been analyzed. Offenses without event data are shown as grey nodes with a no data indicator.

Info

The Lateral Movement lens uses a hierarchical left-to-right layout with physics disabled, rather than the force-directed layout used by other lenses.

docs.title: Relationship Scoring
docs.text:
Graph data is pre-computed during AI analysis (Phase 5) and stored in the offense_relationships table. This means graph rendering is instant — no computation happens at query time.

Each offense pair is scored across five dimensions:

Dimension Weight Signal Shared detection rules 35% Rule ID intersection between the two offenses Same attacker source 30% offense_source equality Shared destination networks 15% destination_networks intersection Shared categories + time proximity 12% Category intersection × time decay factor Lateral movement 8% Destination IPs of A ∩ Source IPs of B

The composite score ranges from 0.0 to 1.0. Only pairs with a score ≥ 0.15 are stored and displayed.

Time decay for campaign topology: full weight (1.0) if the offenses are within 6 hours of each other, linearly decaying to 0.0 at 24 hours apart.

docs.title: Auto-Recommendation
docs.text:
When you open the graph, the backend analyses all stored relationships for the current offense and recommends the lens with the strongest signal. A blue notification banner appears:

Recommended: Attacker Topology 192.168.0.1 links 34 offenses

Click Apply lens to switch to the recommended view, or dismiss the banner and choose manually.
